newsitem.title: PERU: Peru to talk with rebels by Saturday - source.
newsitem.headline: Peru to talk with rebels by Saturday - source.

text.p: Peruvian officials and Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima are likely to meet on Friday or Saturday for fresh face-to-face talks aimed at ending the 58-day-old siege, a government source said on Thursday.
"Today (Thursday) would be difficult. I reckon it will be Friday or Saturday," the source, close to the negotiations, told Reuters.

Government negotiator Domingo Palermo and the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) second-in-command, Rolly Rojas, met for four hours on Tuesday in a Red Cross safe house across the street from the Japanese diplomatic mansion.
At that meeting -- the first since Dec. 28 -- the two sides agreed to carry on with talks but made no obvious progress bridging the gap between their apparently intransigent positions.

Tuesday's resumption of dialogue marked a breakthrough in the crisis. But with the rebels refusing to give up their demand -- which the government rejects -- for the release of hundreds of jailed comrades, a peaceful solution is not expected soon.

As at Tuesday's meeting, a guarantors' commission made up of officials from the Red Cross, the Vatican and the Canadian government will oversee the next talks at the specially rented two-storey home 150 feet (50 meters) from the Japanese residence. Tokyo also is set to have an observer present.

Peru tightened security in the area for the last meeting. A white Red Cross car ferried the rebel to the safe house while special police units in neighbouring homes looked on and sharpshooters on nearby roofs trained their rifles on the building.

President Alberto Fujimori has said the talks with Rojas, a 34-year-old former busfare collector who goes by the nom de guerre "El Arabe" (The Arab), should lead to formal negotiations with rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini.

The rebels originally took more than 500 hostages Dec. 17 during a lavish cocktail party but have freed most of them. The remaining 72 captives in the mined and booby-trapped residence include two Peruvian ministers, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and Fujimori's brother Pedro.
